extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of narratology; literary critics and creative writers studying point of view/focalization
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and analyze focalizers, focalized objects, perceptibility, levels of focalization, and their rhetorical effects in prose narrative (novel, novella, short story). Includes notation conventions and interpretive cues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focalizer type: external (EF) vs internal (CF)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish whether the narrative perspective is an external focalizer (EF) or an internal character focalizer (CF); narratives may switch between EF and CF and several characters can alternate as CFs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note alternations between EF and CF; mark frequent vs rare focalizers (use initials when multiple CFs). Even an apparently objective EF retains an implicit bias. Example: many stories alternate EF and CF; some entire stories may be focalized by an EF.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focalized object (what is being focalized)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify what the character focalizes: characters, objects, landscapes, events—any element can be a focalized object, by EF or CF.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the three diagnostic questions given: 1) What does the character focalize: what is it aimed at? 2) How does it do this: with what attitude does it view things? 3) Who focalizes it: whose focalized object is it? Examples c and d show landscapes and fantasy objects being focalized and interpreted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed vs loose focalizer–focalized combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether combinations of focalizer and focalized object are relatively constant (fixed) or vary greatly (loose).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse fixed pairs because the focalizer shapes the image we receive of the object (e.g., Harold–Indies; Lot–mama Ottilie). Conversely, how a focalizer presents an object reveals traits of the focalizer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive vs impersonal presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the degree to which a presentation includes an interpretation or opinion versus appearing impersonal/objective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for metaphors, clichés, association mechanisms, and colloquial markers that humanize and interpret objects (e.g., 'dressing-jacket of white exudation of bird-droppings'). Deixis (e.g., 'at my side', 'around us') often signals internal position and interpretive stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceptibility of focalized objects: perceptible (p) vs non-perceptible (np)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify whether the focalized object is perceptible to other characters within the fabula (p) or exists only inside a character's mind/dreams/feelings and thus is non-perceptible to others (np).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notation: add 'p' or 'np' to focalizer notation (e.g., CF(woman)–np). Criterion: within the fabula another character should also be able to perceive the object for it to be 'p'. Dreams, fantasies, thoughts, feelings are 'np'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceptibility and power structure between characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Use perceptibility assignments (p/np) to infer relative power or advantage among characters: a character who is allotted both CF–p and CF–np has informational advantage over one who only has CF–p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When one character can reveal inner states (np) while another cannot, the first can manipulate reader perception and the other cannot react to what it doesn't know. First-person novels often exploit this inequality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spoken vs unspoken words (audibility/perceptibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate spoken words (audible/perceptible to others) from unspoken words (thoughts/internal monologues not perceptible to other characters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should track placement of unspoken thoughts (e.g., between dialogue sections) to see how readers are given privileged information relative to characters; this is a common tool for manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focalization levels (F1, F2, ...)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish levels of focalization: a first-level focalizer (F1) is typically external and may delegate focalization to internal focalizers on lower levels (F2, etc.); embedded focalizations should be indexed by level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicate level numerically after the F (e.g., CF2('I')–p). Recognize that 'first-person narrative' and 'third-person narrative' may both contain multiple levels; e.g., a grown-up 'I' EF presenting its younger CF as embedded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attributive signs of level shifts
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify explicit or implicit signs that indicate a shift in focalization level—verbs of perception (see, hear) commonly function as explicit attributive signs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search for verbs like 'saw', 'heard' and other contextual cues; sometimes marking is implicit and must be deduced from surrounding passages (examples: sentence verbs in examples f and g; description in c needed preceding passage to locate shift).

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation and analytic conventions for focalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a systematic notation to record focalizers, focalized objects, perceptibility, levels, and multiple focalizers (use initials for characters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of notation: EF–p, CF('I')–p, CF(woman)–np, CF2('I')–p; for multiple CFs use initials; annotate perceptibility with 'p'/'np' and levels with numbers; useful for tracking relationships like 'Who allows whom to watch whom?'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double and ambiguous focalization (EF1+CF2 vs EF1/CF2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize hinge fragments where a passage is focalized both by EF and CF (double focalization) or where it's unclear who focalizes (ambiguous focalization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notate EF1+CF2 for clear double focalization and EF1/CF2 for ambiguous cases. Example: Chekhov's 'Lady with Lapdog' where sentence 5 is EF1/CF2 or likely EF1+CF2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free indirect/ambiguous focalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify passages where the external focalizer 'watches along' with a character approximating the character's voice without direct speech—comparable to free indirect discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are moments when EF remains but approximates CF language/thought; treat them as ambiguous focalization and examine how closely the narrative voice aligns with the character's perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memory and retrospective focalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat memory as an act of vision situated in the present of remembering; memories are narratively reconstructed and rhetorically overworked, often differing from experienced fabula events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse memory passages for unreliability, fragmentation (trauma), and rhetorical shaping; consider memory as a joint of time and space and as a means of countering external (colonizing) focalizations—e.g., mapping and spatializing memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focalizer reveals more about the focalizer than the object
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess how presentations of objects often yield more information about the focalizer (their experience, tastes, attitudes) than about the object itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples c and d: descriptions of landscape or heaven convey the CF's way of experiencing nature or women. Interpret metaphors and associations as clues to focalizer traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion vs exclusion in humour via focalizer
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether humorous presentation invites the reader into a group formed by the focalizer (inclusive humour) or excludes them (exclusive humour); this also reflects on the focalizer's social positioning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for contrasts between solemn/impersonal registers and personal-everyday turns, and for appeals to group formation; judge whether reader is empowered to accept or reject belonging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspense analyzed through focalization / knowledge distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyse suspense as produced by focalization and the distribution of knowledge between reader and character: four configurations arise (reader– character–; reader+ character–; reader– character+; reader+ character+).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map which party knows the answer and through which focalizer/level the reader learns it. Examples: reader–/char– opens detective-type mysteries; reader+/char– creates 'threat' suspense; reader–/char+ creates secrets revealed gradually (Of Old People); reader+/char+ yields no suspense. Repeated recall and postponement of answers develops suspense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focalization as a primary manipulative and interpretive device
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat focalization as overarching with respect to other narrative aspects: it determines how information about fabula is shaped, presented, and manipulated, and thus influences significance of character image, space, time, and ideology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice, focalization should be central to analyses (even of non-literary texts like newspaper reports) rather than restricting study to semantic content analysis. Ask: What information do we get? How do we get it? How do elements function relative to focalization?

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of spatial deixis and position to locate CF
rubrics_metrics.description: Use spatial expressions and deixis (e.g., 'around us', 'at my side', 'behind') to localize the internal focalizer and infer their vantage point and interpretive relation to the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine words indicating proximity and elevation to detect CF's spatial position; this helps determine whether a description is ostensibly objective or actually interpretive and situated.
